body: When an AI chatbot writes something that sounds right but is not true, people call it a hallucination. Sometimes a chatbot even lists a source, such as a science article, that does not exist at all.

A team at New York University in the USA, led by computer science professor Dennis Shasha, has built a tool called HallucinationNerd to spot this problem. They described it in a science journal on 22 October.

The tool works through a document step by step. First it splits the writing into separate claims. Then it finds the source each claim points to and reads the matching part. Finally it decides whether the source really backs the claim up.

Each claim gets one of six labels: Supported, Partially Supported, Not Supported, Contradicted, Cited article does not exist, or Could not access. In tests on real research papers, the team says it did better than other checking systems.
The tool is a research project, built mainly to help scientists check papers. But the idea behind it is something anyone can use: when you read a fact, check that the source really says it.

discussion: Have you ever found something online that turned out to be wrong? How did you find out?
Why do you think a chatbot might sound just as confident when it is wrong as when it is right?

Some people think AI chatbots should always show where their facts come from. Others say that would make answers slower and longer, and people would not read the sources anyway. What do you think, and why?
Should pupils be allowed to use AI chatbots for homework? Think about the views of a pupil, a teacher and a parent.

Whether cited sources really back up a document's claims
Whether a document has spelling or grammar mistakes
Whether the websites in a document are safe to visit

options: Could not access
Not Supported
Contradicted
Cited article does not exist

quiz.explain: Only the source itself can show whether the fact is backed up. Asking the chatbot again is tempting, but it can confidently repeat the same mistake.
options: Open the link and check it really says the same thing
Ask the chatbot whether it is sure the fact is right
Use it, because a fact with a link must be checked already
Use it if the same chatbot gives the same answer twice

options: Abstraction
Pattern recognition
Decomposition
Debugging

quiz.explain: A chatbot builds text from patterns, choosing words that seem likely to come next, so it can produce a title that only looks real. Broken links are a real problem online, but they are not why a chatbot invents a whole article.
options: It has run out of storage space for real sources
It is copying from a website that has broken links
It builds answers by predicting likely-sounding words
Its programmers typed in fake sources on purpose
quiz.q: Why can an AI chatbot write a source that does not exist?

quiz.explain: Only the two "Not supported" labels add 1, so the count is 2. The tempting 4 counts every claim, but the IF only adds 1 when the label is "Not supported".

stories.standfirst: AI chatbots sometimes invent facts, and even invent the books or articles they say they got them from. Computer scientists have built a tool to check.
stories.whyItMatters: More and more people use AI chatbots for homework and research. A chatbot can sound very confident even when it is wrong. Knowing how to check a source yourself is one of the most useful digital skills there is.

body: Wednesday 14 October was International E-Waste Day. E-waste means electrical and electronic things we throw away. This year the organisers, a group called the WEEE Forum, chose to look at small, cheap gadgets. They call them fast tech, a bit like fast fashion for clothes.

Fast tech includes things like USB adapters, chargers, cables, LED lights, mini fans, electronic toys and earbuds. They are cheap to buy and easy to replace, so people often do not keep them for long.

The WEEE Forum asked over 10,000 adults in 12 European countries about these gadgets. Almost nine in ten owned at least one. More than half could remember a gadget they had used for six months or less. Most people said they were happy with what they bought, and many liked the low price.

Even a tiny gadget usually has a circuit board, wires and sometimes a battery inside. These contain metals and plastics that could be recovered and used again, but only if the gadget is recycled properly. Batteries thrown in the normal bin can also start fires when bin lorries crush them.

The organisers have a simple rule: if it has a plug, a cable, a circuit board or a battery, it is e-waste, however small it is. They suggest asking whether you really need a new gadget, choosing second-hand or repairable ones, and taking old ones to a proper collection point.

Count the chargers, cables and small gadgets in your home or bag. How many do you actually use each week?

Some people say shoppers should buy less. Others say the companies that make and sell gadgets should pay to collect and recycle them. Some say governments should make rules. Who do you think should be most responsible, and why?
A cheap gadget breaks. Fixing it might cost more than buying a new one. What would you do, and what would help you decide?

Small, cheap gadgets that are often used for a short time and then replaced.
A flat board inside a device that connects its electronic parts, such as chips, so they can work together.
Breaking down old items so their materials, like metals and plastics, can be used to make new things.

quiz.explain: Fast tech means small, low-cost electronics like chargers and mini fans that people often replace quickly. It is about how long we keep them, not how fast they run or charge.
options: Gadgets that are delivered the next day
Computers with very fast processors
Cheap gadgets that are used briefly and replaced
Devices that charge in a few minutes

quiz.explain: Anything with a plug, cable, circuit board or battery counts, however small or cheap. A gadget does not need to be online or expensive to be e-waste.

It cost more than £20 when it was new
It can connect to the internet or Wi-Fi
It is made mostly of metal, not plastic

options: The speaker
The button
The LED
The battery
quiz.q: A light-up toy has a button, a speaker, an LED and a battery. Which of these is an input device?

quiz.explain: Crushed batteries can start fires in bin lorries and waste plants. Data is a real worry for phones, but it is not why batteries are dangerous, and batteries can be recycled at proper collection points.
options: Its battery cannot be recycled at all
It will keep using electricity in the bin
Someone could read the data stored on it
The battery could catch fire if it is crushed

options: Charge the battery to 100%
Delete the photos from the gallery app
Back up your data, sign out and reset it
Take off the case and screen protector
quiz.q: You are giving your old tablet to a cousin. What is the most important thing to do first?

stories.standfirst: Mini fans, chargers, cables and earbuds are so cheap that many get thrown away after a few months. Experts have a name for them: fast tech.
stories.whyItMatters: Every gadget is a small computer system made from materials dug out of the ground. Around the world, only about a fifth of e-waste is known to be properly recycled. Small choices about what we buy, keep, fix and throw away really add up.

body: FLIP is an uncrewed rover built by a company called Astrolab in California. It weighs about 480 kilograms and has no driver on board. It is due to travel to the Moon on a robotic lander called Griffin, with launch planned for late 2026.

The rover carries a computer made by Hewlett Packard Enterprise, called Spaceborne Computer-4. It has a CPU and a GPU, a type of chip that is very good at doing lots of small sums at once. The teams say it will be the first time a GPU and AI programs have been tested on the Moon's surface.

The computer will take in data from FLIP's cameras and lidar, a sensor that bounces light off the ground to build a 3D map. AI programs will use this data to help the rover spot craters and find a safe path.
There is no GPS on the Moon. So one experiment will help FLIP work out where it is by matching the hills and craters it can see with a map stored in its memory.

Space is a tough place for computers. Radiation can flip bits in memory, and nights near the south pole are freezing and very long. The computer has no fan, and its software can slow the chip down when radiation levels rise.

groups.explain: Things FLIP will drive past or around. Its AI has to spot craters and boulders to find a safe path.
groups.name: Things on the Moon's surface

groups.explain: Input devices that collect data about the world. Lidar bounces light off the ground to build a 3D map; a gyroscope senses which way the rover is tilting.
groups.name: Sensors a rover can use

groups.explain: The hardware inside FLIP's computer. The GPU is the part that runs the AI programs.
groups.name: Parts of a computer

groups.explain: Bit was the red herring: it sounds like a computer part, but radiation in space can flip a bit from 0 to 1. And the rover is called FLIP!
groups.name: Things you can flip

discussion: Why might it be better for a rover to make some decisions by itself instead of waiting for people on Earth?
Experts warn that AI programs can sometimes give wrong answers. Which rover decisions do you think should always be checked by a human? Why?
FLIP has no GPS. How do you work out where you are when you have no phone or map app?
Design challenge: plan a test on Earth to check that a rover can spot a crater before it reaches the edge. What would you measure, and how would you know if the test passed?
If you could send one sensor to the Moon, what would you want it to measure and why?

keywords.meaning: A vehicle that drives across the surface of a moon or planet, usually controlled from far away.
Graphics processing unit: a chip that does many simple calculations at the same time. It is used for graphics and AI.
A sensor that sends out pulses of light and times how long they take to bounce back, to measure distances.
Working on data where it is collected, instead of sending it all somewhere else first.

parsons.explain: The count starts at 0 before the loop so it is not reset each time. Inside the loop the rover reads a new slope, then the IF only adds 1 when the slope is more than 15. The display comes after END REPEAT so it shows the final total once. Using < 15 would count the safe, gentle slopes instead of the steep ones.

parsons.task: FLIP checks the ground ahead 10 times. Each time, it receives the slope (in degrees) from its sensor. If the slope is more than 15 degrees, it adds 1 to a count of risky spots. At the end it displays the count. One line doesn't belong.
parsons.title: Counting risky spots

quiz.explain: The teams say it will be the first time a GPU and AI programs are tested on the Moon. Rovers have driven on the Moon before, and computers helped guide the Apollo landings back in the 1960s.
options: Driving a vehicle across the Moon's surface
Taking photos of the Moon's south pole
Running AI programs on a GPU
Using a computer to help land a spacecraft
quiz.q: What will FLIP's computer try out on the Moon for the first time?

quiz.explain: GPS works by receiving signals from satellites that circle the Earth, and there is no system like that around the Moon. Radio signals don't need air, so they travel happily through space.
options: There are no GPS satellites circling the Moon
Moon dust would block the rover's GPS antenna
GPS only works where there is air to carry signals
GPS would use up too much of the battery
quiz.q: Why can't FLIP use GPS to find out where it is?

quiz.explain: Cameras and lidar are sensors, which are input devices: they bring data into the computer. They might seem like output because they produce pictures, but the pictures are data going in for the computer to process.
options: Output devices
Input devices
Storage devices
Processing devices
quiz.q: FLIP's cameras and lidar collect information about the ground. What kind of devices are they?

quiz.explain: Matching landmarks you can see to the same landmarks on a map is the same idea FLIP uses. Counting steps can also estimate position, but small errors build up, and it does not compare what you see with a map.
options: Spotting a church and a bridge, then finding them both on a paper map
Counting your steps from your front door to guess how far you have gone
Asking a friend to send you your location on their phone
Following spoken turn-by-turn directions from a satnav
quiz.q: FLIP finds its position by matching the craters it sees with a stored map. Which everyday method is most like this?
quiz.strand: Understanding the world through computational thinking

quiz.explain: The connection to Earth has limited bandwidth, so sending only the useful results saves time and lets the rover react quickly. Computers on Earth can open the photos fine; the problem is getting all of them there.
options: Computers on Earth cannot open photos taken on the Moon
It means the rover needs no cameras to see
The rover stores pictures better than computers on Earth
The link to Earth can only send a limited amount of data
quiz.q: Why is it useful for FLIP to process its camera data on board instead of sending every picture to Earth?

quiz.explain: The photo takes 1.3 seconds to reach Earth and the reply takes 1.3 seconds to come back, so 1.3 + 1.3 = 2.6 seconds. Only counting one direction gives 1.3 seconds, which is the most common slip.
options: About 1.3 seconds
About 2.6 seconds
About 3.9 seconds
About 0.65 seconds
quiz.q: Challenge: a radio signal takes about 1.3 seconds to travel from the Moon to Earth. FLIP sends a photo and a controller replies instantly. What is the shortest time before FLIP gets the reply?
quiz.strand: Understanding the world through computational thinking

stories.imageAlt: Illustration of a supermarket fridge connected to the internet, with its thermometer rising into the red.
stories.headline: Hackers turn up the heat on supermarket fridges
stories.standfirst: A cyber attack in France switched hundreds of shop freezers to scorching temperatures. What happened, and could it happen to the devices in your home?
body: Imagine walking into a supermarket and finding the freezer aisle warm. That is what happened at hundreds of shops in France on Monday 12 October, after hackers broke into the computer systems that control their fridges and freezers.

Big supermarket fridges are not like the one in your kitchen. Many are linked to a central computer, so staff can check and change the temperature from anywhere using the internet. The attackers used that remote control to turn the temperature right up, in some cases to around 50°C. That is hotter than a scorching summer's day.

More than 400 stores were affected, including branches of well-known chains such as Carrefour, Intermarché and Coopérative U. Fresh and frozen food had to be thrown away, and a few overheated machines even caught fire.

The company whose software runs the fridges said most of the affected equipment was old and no longer received security updates. Updates fix weak spots that attackers can use, so a machine that stops getting them becomes an easier target. After the attack, some shops unplugged their fridge systems from the internet.
Police in Paris are investigating. Nobody yet knows who did it, or why.
stories.whyItMatters: More and more everyday objects are connected to the internet: doorbells, speakers, toys, even fridges. Together they are called the Internet of Things. Each one is a small computer, and every computer needs looking after with strong passwords and regular updates.

keywords.meaning: Everyday objects that connect to the internet so they can send data or be controlled from far away.
A fix sent out by a company to close weak spots in its software before attackers can use them.
Controlling a computer or device from somewhere else, over a network.
An attempt to break into, damage or take control of computers or data without permission.

discussion: The fridges could be controlled over the internet so staff could manage them from anywhere. What are the good things about that? What are the risks?
List five devices in your home or school that connect to the internet. Which one would cause the biggest problem if it was hacked, and why?
The software company had stopped sending updates to the old fridges. Who should be responsible for keeping an old device safe: the maker, the shop, or both?
Some shops unplugged their fridges from the internet after the attack. Is disconnecting always the best answer? What would they lose?
Design challenge: a fridge is getting too warm. Write the steps an alarm system should follow, using IF and THEN.

quiz.q: What did the hackers change on the supermarket fridges?
options: Prices on the electronic shelf labels
Customers' loyalty card details
The card payment machines
The temperature
quiz.explain: The attackers used the fridges' remote control system to turn the temperature right up. Prices, payments and customer data were not what they changed.

quiz.q: Why were these fridges an easier target for attackers?
options: They were connected by Wi-Fi instead of cables
They were old and no longer got security updates
They were made by a company outside France
They were switched off overnight for cleaning
quiz.explain: Updates fix weak spots in software. Equipment that stops getting them keeps its weak spots for attackers to find. Wi-Fi or cables, either can be attacked if the software is weak.

quiz.q: A fridge you can control from a phone app is an example of…
options: Artificial intelligence
Cloud storage
The Internet of Things
A local area network (LAN)
quiz.explain: Everyday objects that connect to the internet are called the Internet of Things, or IoT. The fridge might use a LAN or the cloud, but the device itself is an IoT device.

quiz.q: A fridge's controller follows this rule: IF temperature > 5°C THEN switch cooling ON. The sensor reads 8°C. What happens?
options: Cooling switches ON
Cooling switches OFF
Nothing happens, because 8 is not equal to 5
The rule keeps repeating until the reading is 5°C
quiz.explain: 8 is greater than 5, so the condition is true and the THEN part runs once. This decision is called selection. Repeating would need a loop, which this rule doesn't have.
quiz.strand: Understanding the world through computational thinking

quiz.q: Which is the best way to keep a smart device at home safer?
options: Turn off Bluetooth when it isn't being used
Clear its history every week
Change the default password and install updates
Only use it while connected to mobile data
quiz.explain: Default passwords are easy to find online, and updates close known weak spots. The other ideas don't stop an attacker who can reach the device over the internet.

quiz.q: Challenge: computers store numbers in binary. Which binary number equals 50?
quiz.explain: 110010 = 32 + 16 + 2 = 50. Check the others: 101100 is 44, 110100 is 52 and 110001 is 49. Each place is worth double the one to its right: 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

stories.headline: The drone that plans around things it can't predict
stories.standfirst: Engineers at MIT have built a flight planner that steers drones safely past moving obstacles, even in places nobody has mapped.
body: Flying a drone through an empty field is easy. Flying one through a forest during a wildfire, or down a busy street, is much harder, because things keep moving and you can't know where they'll be next.

Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in the USA have created a system called SANDO to solve this. It uses the drone's own cameras and sensors to spot obstacles and track how they move.

Here's the clever part. SANDO doesn't try to guess exactly where a moving object will go. Instead, it works out the fastest that object could possibly travel, and draws an imaginary bubble around it showing every place it might reach. The longer into the future it looks, the bigger the bubble gets.

Next, it builds a safe tunnel of open space that avoids all the bubbles, then picks the quickest route through that tunnel. As the drone flies, it keeps repeating these steps, updating the tunnel and the route whenever something changes.

In computer simulations, SANDO reached its goal faster than other planners without a single crash. It then flew 12 real test flights and avoided every moving obstacle. The team thinks it could help with search and rescue, fighting wildfires and delivering parcels.
stories.whyItMatters: Robots that move around people need to be safe as well as clever. SANDO shows how breaking a hard problem into clear steps, and repeating them many times a second, lets a computer make safe decisions in a world that keeps changing.

keywords.meaning: A set of clear steps for solving a problem or completing a task.
A device that measures something in the world, like distance, light or movement, and turns it into data.
Able to make decisions and act without a person controlling it.
A computer model of a real situation, used to test ideas safely before trying them for real.

discussion: SANDO plans for the worst case: the fastest an obstacle could move. When else do people plan for the worst case in everyday life?
Would you feel safe with drones delivering parcels in your street? What would make you trust them more?
The team tested in simulations before real flights. Why might engineers test this way first?
Search and rescue, wildfires, deliveries: which use do you think is most important, and why?
Try it: one person walks slowly around the room while another plans a route across it. What rules did you use to stay safe?

quiz.q: What does SANDO's imaginary 'bubble' around an obstacle show?
options: Exactly where the obstacle will be one second later
Every place the obstacle could possibly reach
The area the drone's camera can see
How close the drone can fly before it must land
quiz.explain: SANDO doesn't predict one exact spot. It uses the fastest the object could move and covers every place it might reach, then keeps the drone out of that bubble.

quiz.q: The drone's camera spots an obstacle. In 'input → process → output', the camera is the…
options: Process
Output
Input
Storage
quiz.explain: The camera collects data from the world, so it's an input. Working out the route is the process, and spinning the rotors to move is the output.

quiz.q: SANDO keeps updating its route again and again while flying. In programming, repeating steps is called…
options: Sequence
Selection
A variable
Repetition (a loop)
quiz.explain: Repeating a set of instructions is called repetition, or a loop. Sequence is steps in order, and selection is choosing with IF.
quiz.strand: Understanding the world through computational thinking

quiz.q: Why would the bubble around an obstacle get bigger the further ahead SANDO plans?
options: There is more time for the obstacle to travel further
The drone's sensors get less accurate as it flies
The obstacle is moving closer to the camera
The drone must fly faster later in the journey
quiz.explain: The more time that passes, the further something could travel, so the area it might reach keeps growing.
quiz.strand: Understanding the world through computational thinking

quiz.q: Why did the researchers test SANDO in simulations first?
options: Simulations are always more accurate than real flights
To test it safely and cheaply before risking real drones
Drones aren't allowed to fly outdoors in the USA
A simulation doesn't need any code to run
quiz.explain: A simulation lets engineers try thousands of situations without crashing anything. It is useful but not perfect, which is why they still did 12 real flights.
quiz.strand: Designing, building and testing computing solutions

parsons.title: Drone flight loop
parsons.task: The drone starts 100 metres from its goal. Each time round the loop it should check its sensor, replan if something is near, then move 10 metres closer. When it arrives it shows a message. One line doesn't belong.
parsons.explain: The distance must be set before the loop tests it. Inside the loop the drone senses, decides, then moves. Subtracting 10 brings it closer; adding 10 would move it further away and the loop would never end. "Goal reached" goes after END WHILE so it only shows once.

stories.imageAlt: Illustration of a computer processor chip with a grid of 80 small squares representing its cores.
stories.headline: Europe's own brain chip arrives for its fastest supercomputer
stories.standfirst: A processor with 80 cores, designed in Europe, is being fitted into JUPITER, a giant computer in Germany that can do a billion billion sums every second.
body: Every computer has a CPU, the central processing unit. It is the part that carries out instructions, like a brain following a recipe. Most of the CPUs in Europe's biggest computers have been designed by companies in the USA.

In September, a French company called SiPearl delivered the first samples of a new CPU called Rhea1. It was designed in Europe, and it is being built into JUPITER, Europe's fastest working supercomputer, at a research centre in Jülich, Germany.
Rhea1 has 80 cores. A core is like a separate worker inside the chip. With 80 of them, the chip can split a huge job into pieces and work on many pieces at the same time.

JUPITER is an exascale supercomputer. That means it can do at least a billion billion calculations every second. Scientists use machines like this to predict the weather, study climate change, design medicines and train AI.
Europe wanted its own chip so it relies less on other countries for important technology. A second chip, Rhea2, is planned for another supercomputer in France.
stories.whyItMatters: Supercomputers help answer some of the biggest questions in science. Who designs and makes the chips inside them matters too, because countries want to be sure they can always get the technology they depend on.

keywords.meaning: Central processing unit: the part of a computer that carries out program instructions.
One processing unit inside a CPU. More cores means more tasks can run at the same time.
A very powerful computer made from thousands of processors working together.
Able to do at least a billion billion (10^18) calculations every second.

discussion: Why might a country or region want to design its own computer chips instead of buying them from elsewhere?
If a supercomputer could answer one question for you, what would you ask it to work on?
Splitting a big job between 80 workers sounds faster. Can you think of a job that does not get faster with more workers?
Supercomputers use huge amounts of electricity. How should scientists balance this against what they discover?

quiz.q: What does CPU stand for?
options: Computer Processing Unit
Central Processing Unit
Central Program Utility
Core Processing Unit
quiz.explain: CPU stands for Central Processing Unit, the part that carries out the instructions in a program.

quiz.q: How many cores does the new Rhea1 chip have?
quiz.explain: Rhea1 has 80 cores, so it can work on many parts of a job at the same time.

quiz.q: Why do lots of cores help a computer finish big jobs faster?
options: Each core stores a different part of the job's files
More cores give the computer more memory
Each core makes single instructions run faster
Different parts of the job can run at the same time
quiz.explain: Splitting work so several parts happen at once is called parallel processing. Cores don't add memory or storage, and one instruction still runs at the same speed.

quiz.q: A job has 80 equal pieces. Each core does one piece in 1 second. Roughly how long do 80 cores take, compared with 1 core?
options: About 1 second instead of 80
About 40 seconds instead of 80
About 79 seconds instead of 80
80 seconds either way
quiz.explain: All 80 pieces run at once, so it takes about 1 second. Real jobs rarely split this perfectly, but the idea is the same.
quiz.strand: Understanding the world through computational thinking

quiz.q: Challenge: which binary number equals 80?
quiz.explain: 1010000 = 64 + 16 = 80. The others are 96, 72 and 84. Place values from the left are 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

parsons.title: Sharing work between cores
parsons.task: A job has 80 pieces and the chip has 8 free cores. Each round, every core finishes one piece. Put the lines in order to count how many rounds the job takes. One line doesn't belong.
parsons.explain: Both counters are set up before the loop. Each time round, 8 pieces are finished and 1 is added to rounds. The answer is 10. Taking 1 away from rounds would count backwards and give -10.
